moments.title: Traditional date of first Ancient Olympics
moments.body:
Ancient Greek sources record stadion races at Olympia continuing into the late Roman period.

The Games are abolished around 393 CE under Theodosius I.
moments.takeaway: Athletic competition existed as a religious and civic institution long before modern sport.

moments.title: First modern Olympics
moments.body:
Approximately 240 male athletes from 14 nations compete in 43 events.

Women first compete in tennis and golf at Paris 1900.
moments.takeaway: The modern Games revived a tradition while adding new institutional structures.

moments.title: First Paralympic Games
moments.body: Building on Guttmann's 1948 Stoke Mandeville games for spinal-injured veterans, the first official Paralympics are held in Rome with 400 athletes from 23 nations.
moments.takeaway: Para-sport began as rehabilitative medicine and grew into a major international movement.

now.title: The Olympic movement today
now.body: Recent Games involve over 10,000 athletes. Cost overruns, doping scandals and disputes over participation policies dominate governance debates.
now.open_questions: How should cost and environmental impact be weighed against the cultural value of hosting? How should categories be defined for elite competition?

items.reflection: The modern Olympics often present themselves as direct heirs of antiquity, but the institutional gap is huge and the reinvention is recent.

moments.title: Title IX signed
moments.body: Title IX of the Education Amendments prohibits sex discrimination in federally funded education programmes, including athletics.
moments.takeaway: A general civil rights law had outsized effects on sport participation.

moments.title: First Women's World Cup
moments.body:
Twelve teams compete in Guangdong; the United States wins.

Women's football grows steadily in subsequent decades, alongside ongoing debates over pay and investment.
moments.takeaway: International women's competitions consolidated after national-level shifts.

moments.title: Every Olympic nation includes women
moments.body: Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Brunei send female athletes for the first time, meaning every participating nation has female athletes.
moments.takeaway: Institutional integration of women athletes was achieved at the world level only in the 21st century.

now.title: Sport participation today
now.body: Female participation has risen sharply since the 1970s, alongside continuing gaps in pay, coverage and facility access. Questions of eligibility in women's competition are politically and scientifically contested.
now.open_questions: How should world federations balance fairness, inclusion and safety in eligibility policies?

items.reflection: Sport policy is one of the clearest examples of how legal frameworks reshape participation across a single generation.

moments.title: Hill and Lupton on oxygen uptake
moments.body: Hill (Nobel laureate 1922) and Lupton describe maximal oxygen uptake as a determinant of endurance performance.
moments.takeaway: Modern sport science began in physiology labs working on energy metabolism.

moments.title: Saltin and Astrand on training
moments.body: Scandinavian research establishes detailed relationships between training, cardiac output and endurance.
moments.takeaway: Cross-national research consortia produced the modern training evidence base.

moments.title: 'Live high, train low' published
moments.body: Their study supports a protocol where athletes live at altitude but train at lower elevations, balancing adaptation and intensity.
moments.takeaway: Elite-level training innovations often emerge from carefully controlled physiological studies.

now.title: Sport science today
now.body: Wearable sensors and biomechanics labs allow individualised monitoring. Open questions remain about overtraining markers and long-term injury risk.
now.open_questions: How well do laboratory measures predict competitive performance? What ethical limits apply to performance technologies short of doping?

items.reflection: Sport science walks a line between performance enhancement, athlete welfare and the integrity of competition.
